headline: Moving the styled primitives behind a module boundary costs the compiled lanes a few percent and nothing else, so per-module compilation survives the way design systems actually ship components.

microbench.why: The workload is byte-identical to `tabs` in DOM and CSS, so the ordering is too: `vanilla` at 0.806 ms/1k, `stylex-layers` 0.875 and `next-yak-css-9.7` 0.899, all of them rendering plain elements with classes that were resolved during the build. `bamboo` (2.17) and `panda` (2.41) again report no styling work and lose in react-dom, 75.9 and 89.5 ms of their JS windows. Nothing here depends on file layout for the runtime libraries: `emotion` (5.93) and `styled-components` (3.93) match their `tabs` figures to within a few percent.

autocannon.why: `vanilla` 719 req/s and `next-yak-css-9.7` 637 on 2.37-2.69 kB, then the atomic and utility lanes at 191-248 on kilobyte-scale class attributes, then the hashing lanes. Every figure is within a few percent of the `tabs` twin, which is the finding: the module boundary does not change what is served.

attribution.why: `vanilla` (1.37 ms) and `next-yak-css-9.7` (1.41, with 0.256 ms of library time) sit at the react-dom floor, and `stylex-layers` joins them at 1.42 with no library slice and 0.351 ms of component self-time merging static class constants. `bamboo` at 3.04 ms and `panda` at 3.64 report zero library time and spend 2.80 and 3.23 ms in React writing their names. next-yak's styled API costs 2.07 ms here with a 0.673 ms library slice against 2.21 ms in the single-file twin, so the imported primitives cost it nothing on the server.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

hydrate.why: 48.1-63.6 ms of pure JS for every lane with a static sheet, zero style and zero layout in the span. `goober` (200 ms) and `styled-components` (202 ms) inject during hydration, 2.26 and 2.25 ms of recalculation plus a 3.5 ms layout, and present 18 frames instead of one.

inp.why: One tab switch, under 1.1 ms of span JS in every static-class lane, a 6.8-7.8 ms cluster that is one measurement wide. `emotion` at 28.1 ms spends 0.845 ms of the span inside `@emotion/hash`, and `panda-props` at 27.1 re-resolves style props for the group that changed.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

mount.why: 95.6-113 ms for everything that ships a sheet. `emotion` (232 ms), `styled-components` (209) and `goober` (207) build theirs before first paint. `panda` mounts at 102 ms because its `css()` calls sit at module scope and resolve once at import.

renderTiming.why: Counts tie at one recalculation everywhere, and the same three injecting lanes run two layouts and present 18 frames. Their recalculation costs 1.65-1.83 ms against the 0.848-0.993 ms of every lane that loads a finished sheet.

payload.why: Byte-for-byte the `tabs` figures: 2.37 kB for the css-prop fold, 16.1 kB for `panda`, 22.0 for `cnfast`. The module boundary changes what the compiler can see, not what it emits, and the emitted CSS and markup are identical in both cases.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

nsweep.why: At 4,000 groups `stylex` (31.6 ms) and `vanilla` (31.7) lead and `next-yak-css-9.7` follows at 36.0. That last figure is the whole cost of the boundary: 33.5 ms for the same workload written in one file. `panda` (121 ms), `styled-components` (168) and `emotion` (194) scale with n regardless of where the code lives.

crossCase: Against its single-file twin, the Example `tabs` shown above, the module boundary costs `next-yak-css-9.7` 0.858 to 0.899 ms/1k on the microbench and 33.5 to 36.0 ms at n=4,000, roughly 5-8%, with byte-identical 2.37 kB payloads. next-yak's styled API moves 64.3 to 70.5 ms on the same sweep. Per-module compilation cannot follow a styled component across the import, so a runtime wrapper survives where it would otherwise fold; what the numbers say is that the surviving wrapper is cheap, not that the boundary is invisible.
